title: A Museum Teaches Us to Move Through Complexity Without Seeing Everything All at Once
author: Nicole Williams
summary: Nicole Williams uses the museum as a model for leading complex work. A museum gives visitors a threshold, a first room and then the next, with signage and sightlines that let them choose a next move without being shown everything at once. She argues that organizations tend to assume that if everyone could see the whole picture, decisions and coordination would improve, so they add dashboards, documentation and meetings, which confuses information with clarity and can cause overload. She separates comprehension, knowing the whole, from orientation, knowing enough about where you are, your dependencies and the next move. Plans, dashboards and org charts are partial maps, so organizations need signage at the thresholds where one team's output becomes another's dependency. She offers four orienting questions and is candid that the leap from museum research to organizational design is her own interpretation.
points: The central claim is that complex work needs orientation rather than full comprehension, meaning enough information to make the next good move.
More dashboards, documents and meetings can create overload because they substitute information for clarity.
Signage at each junction helps visitors more than a paper guide handed over at the entrance, and the organizational parallel is clear markers at team and policy handoffs.
Four questions test whether work is well signposted: where am I and why does this exist, which decisions are mine, how do I escalate, and is there room to stop and reconsider.
Williams flags that the museum-to-organization step is interpretation, not proof, which keeps the argument honest.
quotes: Museums are a perfect model for understanding complex work because they give you enough orientation to make the next move in the environment. You learn the museum and art by moving through it.
But it confuses information with clarity. It can create information overload when actually what’s needed is more clarity for better decisions.

If we want to know the whole, we want comprehension. If we need to know enough about where we are today, the current surroundings (dependencies), and what the next moves should be, then we want orientation.
Signage at each junction does more for viewing than a paper guide handed to visitors at the entrance.
A project plan is a partial view of the project. A dashboard shows the parts someone chose to measure, and an org chart doesn’t show who people go to when something breaks.
In museums, visitors follow the chronology, wander to bright rooms, follow their favorite artist, or sit for hours looking at a single painting. Nothing is dictated, everything designed.
I’m not saying museums prove how organizations should run complex work. They don’t. Research tells us how people move through exhibition spaces.
People need a shared direction, boundaries, and lattitude when conditions change.
